lessons.title: What Is Health and Safety?
lessons.summary: This foundation module introduces the essential ideas every worker needs before starting or supporting workplace activities. It uses simple English, practical examples and short knowledge checks.

sections.heading: Learning Objective
points: Explain workplace health and safety.
Understand why safety is important.
Recognize that safety is a shared responsibility.
Take basic action after noticing danger.

sections.heading: Core Lesson
points: Workplace health and safety means protecting people from injuries, illnesses and other harm caused by work. It includes safe workplaces, hazard identification, risk control, safe equipment, training, emergency preparation and reporting.

Health protects people from illness or long-term harm such as noise-induced hearing loss, dust exposure, chemicals, poor posture and stress. Safety protects people from immediate events such as falls, electric shock, fire, moving equipment and machinery incidents.
Safety is not only PPE. PPE is one part of a complete system and is normally the last level in the Hierarchy of Controls.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
points: Prevents injuries and occupational illness.
Saves lives and protects property.
Reduces delays and financial loss.
Builds worker confidence and productivity.
Supports legal and organizational compliance.
Helps everyone return home safely.

sections.heading: Shared Responsibility
points: Employers must provide a safe workplace, assess risks, provide suitable equipment, information, training, supervision, PPE and emergency arrangements. Workers must follow instructions, use equipment correctly, wear required PPE, report hazards and avoid unsafe acts.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: Ahmed finds a damaged electrical cable with visible internal wires. He must stop using it, prevent others from using it, attach a Do Not Use identification where the procedure allows, and report it. Only an authorized person may inspect or repair it.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of workplace health and safety?
options: Prevent people from being harmed by work
questions.explanation: It protects people from work-related injury, illness and harm.

questions.prompt: Which is a workplace health hazard?
questions.explanation: Noise exposure can permanently damage hearing.

questions.prompt: What should you do with a seriously damaged cable?
questions.explanation: Damaged equipment must be taken out of use and controlled.

lessons.title: Hazard and Risk Difference
lessons.summary: This foundation module introduces the essential ideas every worker needs before starting or supporting workplace activities. It uses simple English, practical examples and short knowledge checks.

sections.heading: Key Definitions
points: A hazard is anything with the potential to cause injury, illness, property damage, environmental damage or business interruption.
Risk is the combination of the chance that harm will occur and how serious the harm could be. A common simple approach is: Risk = Likelihood x Severity.

sections.heading: Examples
points: Open roof edge (hazard): a person could fall and suffer fatal injury (risk).
Damaged cable (hazard): electric shock, burns or fire (risk).
Moving forklift (hazard): a worker could be struck or crushed (risk).
Excessive noise (hazard): permanent hearing damage (risk).
Easy memory rule: Hazard asks, 'What can cause harm?' Risk asks, 'How could harm occur, how likely is it, and how serious could it be?'

sections.heading: Risk Can Change
points: A chemical remains a hazard, but its risk may be reduced when it is sealed, labelled, correctly stored and handled under controlled conditions. Controls may reduce likelihood, severity, or both, depending on the hazard.

sections.heading: Basic Risk Assessment
points: Identify hazards.
Decide who may be harmed and how.
Review existing controls.
Evaluate likelihood and severity.
Add further controls.
Record and communicate the assessment.
Review when work or conditions change.

questions.prompt: What is a hazard?
options: Anything with potential to cause harm
questions.explanation: A hazard is a source or condition with potential to cause harm.

questions.prompt: Which two factors commonly evaluate risk?
questions.explanation: Risk considers probability and consequence.

questions.prompt: Which correctly identifies a damaged cable?
options: Hazard: cable; risk: shock, burns or fire
questions.explanation: The damaged cable is the hazard; harm is the risk outcome.

lessons.title: Common Workplace Hazards
lessons.summary: This foundation module introduces the essential ideas every worker needs before starting or supporting workplace activities. It uses simple English, practical examples and short knowledge checks.

sections.heading: Physical Hazards
points: Examples: Noise, vibration, heat, cold, poor lighting, radiation and slippery surfaces.
Possible harm: Hearing damage, heat stress, falls and long-term illness.

sections.heading: Mechanical and Safety Hazards
points: Examples: Unguarded machines, rotating parts, sharp tools, suspended loads, vehicles, excavations and work at height.
Possible harm: Cuts, crushing, amputation, falls and fatal injury.

sections.heading: Electrical Hazards
points: Examples: Damaged cables, exposed conductors, overloads, poor grounding, wet conditions and overhead lines.
Possible harm: Shock, burns, fire, explosion and death.

sections.heading: Chemical Hazards
points: Examples: Solvents, paint, cement, fuel, fumes, gases and acids.
Possible harm: Burns, poisoning, breathing problems, cancer, fire or explosion.

sections.heading: Biological Hazards
points: Examples: Bacteria, viruses, mould, contaminated water, waste and used needles.
Possible harm: Infection, allergy, skin disease and respiratory illness.

sections.heading: Ergonomic Hazards
points: Examples: Heavy lifting, repetition, awkward posture, overhead work and poor workstation design.
Possible harm: Back injury, strain, joint pain and fatigue.

sections.heading: Fire and Explosion Hazards
points: Examples: Ignition sources, fuels, gas leaks, hot work and poor flammable storage.
Possible harm: Burns, smoke inhalation, explosion, damage and death.

sections.heading: Psychosocial Hazards
points: Examples: Excessive workload, fatigue, bullying, poor communication and uncontrolled lone work.
Possible harm: Stress, anxiety, poor concentration and unsafe decisions.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: A worker is grinding in poor ventilation. The guard is missing, the cable is damaged and flammable material is nearby. This one task contains mechanical, electrical, health, noise, flying-particle and fire hazards. Stop the task until all hazards are controlled.

questions.prompt: Which is an ergonomic hazard?
questions.explanation: Poor lifting posture may cause musculoskeletal injury.

questions.prompt: Which is an electrical hazard?
questions.explanation: Exposed conductors can cause shock, burns or fire.

questions.prompt: Grinding is taking place near flammable material. What should happen first?
options: Stop and control the fire hazard
questions.explanation: Uncontrolled hot work must stop.

lessons.title: Employer and Employee Responsibilities
lessons.summary: This foundation module introduces the essential ideas every worker needs before starting or supporting workplace activities. It uses simple English, practical examples and short knowledge checks.

sections.heading: Employer Responsibilities
points: Provide and maintain a workplace that is safe so far as reasonably practicable.
Identify hazards, assess risks and implement suitable controls.
Provide safe plant, tools, access and systems of work.
Provide information, instruction, training and competent supervision.
Consult workers and communicate relevant safety information.
Provide emergency arrangements, first aid and suitable welfare facilities.
Provide required PPE without using it as a substitute for higher-level controls.
Investigate incidents and improve controls.

sections.heading: Employee Responsibilities
points: Take reasonable care of their own health and safety and that of others.
Follow procedures, permits, training and supervisor instructions.
Use equipment and PPE correctly and never defeat safety devices.
Attend required training and ask when instructions are unclear.
Report hazards, defects, near misses, incidents and symptoms of occupational illness.
Do not work while impaired by alcohol, drugs, severe fatigue or a condition that creates danger.
Stop and report serious and immediate danger in line with company procedure.
Cooperate with investigations and corrective actions.

sections.heading: Supervisor Responsibilities
points: Supervisors translate plans into safe work. They confirm competence, permits, equipment condition, controls, communication and emergency readiness before work, then monitor the activity and stop deviations.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: A supervisor tells an untrained worker to operate a MEWP to save time. The worker should not operate it. The employer must provide competent operators and safe systems; the supervisor must verify competence; the worker must refuse unauthorized operation and report the situation.

questions.prompt: Who is responsible for workplace safety?
questions.explanation: Safety duties are shared, although authority and duties differ.

questions.prompt: What should a worker do when instructions are unclear?
questions.explanation: Work should not start without understanding the safe method.

questions.prompt: Which is a supervisor responsibility?
options: Allow any person to operate equipment
questions.explanation: Supervisors must verify readiness and monitor work.

lessons.title: Reporting Hazards, Near Misses and Incidents
lessons.summary: This foundation module introduces the essential ideas every worker needs before starting or supporting workplace activities. It uses simple English, practical examples and short knowledge checks.

sections.heading: Important Definitions
points: Hazard report: information about an unsafe condition or act before harm occurs. Near miss: an unplanned event that did not cause injury or damage but had the potential to do so. Incident: an unplanned event that caused or could have caused injury, illness, damage or loss. Emergency reporting follows the site's emergency procedure and takes priority.

sections.heading: Why Reporting Matters
points: Allows action before someone is harmed.
Reveals recurring problems and weak controls.
Supports investigation and organizational learning.
Helps meet company and legal notification duties.
Creates a positive reporting culture when handled fairly.

sections.heading: Basic Reporting Process
points: If there is immediate danger, stop work and warn affected people.
Raise the alarm or contact emergency services according to site procedure.
Provide first aid only within your training and protect yourself.
Make the area safe without creating another risk.
Inform the supervisor or responsible person immediately.
Record facts: what, where, when, who, conditions and immediate action.
Preserve the scene and evidence when safe and required.
Support investigation; do not blame, hide facts or change evidence.
Track corrective actions to closure.

sections.heading: Quality of a Report
points: Write facts, not assumptions. Use clear location, time, activity, observed condition and immediate action. Avoid emotional or blaming language. Photos may help when permitted, safe and compliant with privacy and site rules.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: A spanner falls from a scaffold but misses a worker. No one is injured. This is a near miss and must be reported. The area should be controlled, work stopped, tool tethering and toe boards checked, and causes investigated before restarting.

questions.prompt: What is a near miss?
options: An event with no harm but potential for harm
questions.explanation: Near misses provide an opportunity to prevent future injury.

questions.prompt: What should be written in a report?
questions.explanation: Accurate facts support a fair investigation.

questions.prompt: A tool falls but injures nobody. What should happen?
options: Report and investigate the near miss
questions.explanation: The event had serious potential and controls may have failed.

lessons.title: Basic Emergency Actions
lessons.summary: This foundation module introduces the essential ideas every worker needs before starting or supporting workplace activities. It uses simple English, practical examples and short knowledge checks.

sections.heading: Emergency Priorities
points: Protect yourself - do not become another casualty.
Raise the alarm immediately.
Call the correct emergency contact and provide clear information.
Stop work and isolate energy only if trained, authorized and safe.
Help others only within your competence.
Evacuate by the designated route to the assembly point.
Follow instructions from emergency wardens and responders.
Do not re-enter until officially authorized.

sections.heading: Information to Communicate
points: Your name and contact method.
Exact location and access point.
Type of emergency.
Number and condition of casualties, if known.
Hazards still present, such as fire, gas, electricity or unstable structure.
Assistance already provided.

sections.heading: Fire
points: Raise the alarm, stop work and evacuate. Use an extinguisher only if trained, the fire is small and manageable, the correct extinguisher is available, there is a safe escape route, and site procedure permits. Never fight a fire that is spreading or producing dangerous smoke.

sections.heading: Medical Emergency
points: Call for help, make the area safe and send someone to guide responders. Do not move a casualty unless leaving them creates greater danger. Provide first aid only within your training. Do not give food, drink or medication unless directed by qualified medical personnel.

sections.heading: Gas Release or Unknown Atmosphere
points: Do not enter or attempt a rescue without the correct training, authorization and equipment. Raise the alarm, move crosswind or upwind as instructed, avoid ignition sources and report to the designated assembly point.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: A fire alarm sounds while a worker is using a power tool. The worker should stop safely if this can be done immediately, leave by the designated route, avoid lifts, go to the assembly point and remain available for the roll call. Personal belongings must not delay evacuation.

questions.prompt: What is the first priority in an emergency?
options: Protect yourself and raise the alarm
questions.explanation: A responder must avoid becoming another casualty and alert others.

questions.prompt: When may a worker use a fire extinguisher?
options: Only when trained, conditions are safe and procedure permits
questions.explanation: Firefighting is only appropriate under controlled, permitted conditions.

questions.prompt: When may people re-enter after evacuation?
questions.explanation: Emergency control personnel decide when re-entry is safe.

lessons.title: Hierarchy of Controls
lessons.summary: This foundation module introduces the essential ideas every worker needs before starting or supporting workplace activities. It uses simple English, practical examples and short knowledge checks.

sections.heading: Purpose
points: The Hierarchy of Controls ranks risk-control methods from most effective to least effective. Higher-level controls act on the hazard itself and should be considered before relying on behaviour or PPE.

sections.heading: 1. Elimination
points: Remove the hazard completely, such as completing an assembly at ground level instead of working at height.

sections.heading: 2. Substitution
points: Replace the hazard with a safer option, such as using a less hazardous chemical.

sections.heading: 3. Engineering Controls
points: Physically separate people from danger using guardrails, machine guards, ventilation or enclosures.

sections.heading: 4. Administrative Controls
points: Change how work is performed using procedures, permits, training, signs, supervision or job rotation.

sections.heading: 5. PPE
points: Protect the individual with suitable helmets, gloves, eye, hearing, respiratory or fall-protection equipment.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: Workers create dust while cutting material. First consider pre-cut material, then a lower-dust method, on-tool extraction or wet cutting, restricted access, training, supervision and suitable respiratory and eye protection. More than one control may be required.

questions.prompt: Which is the most effective control level?
questions.explanation: Elimination removes the hazard completely.

questions.prompt: Which is an engineering control?
questions.explanation: A guardrail physically separates people from a fall hazard.

questions.prompt: Why should PPE not be the only control when higher controls are practicable?
options: PPE relies on correct human use and does not remove the hazard
questions.explanation: PPE is important but less reliable than removing or isolating the hazard.

lessons.title: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
lessons.summary: This foundation module introduces the essential ideas every worker needs before starting or supporting workplace activities. It uses simple English, practical examples and short knowledge checks.

sections.heading: Purpose and Types
points: PPE is equipment worn or held to reduce exposure to a specific hazard. It supports stronger controls and is normally the last level in the Hierarchy of Controls.
Safety helmet and required chin strap.
Safety footwear.
Safety glasses, goggles or face shield.
Task-specific gloves.
Hearing protection.
High-visibility clothing.
Suitable respiratory protective equipment.
Full-body harness and compatible fall-protection equipment.

sections.heading: Correct Selection and Use
points: Base selection on the risk assessment and manufacturer information.
Confirm correct size, fit and compatibility.
Inspect before use and at required intervals.
Never modify or use damaged/expired PPE.
Clean and store equipment correctly.
Understand limitations and replacement requirements.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: Ordinary fabric gloves are selected for a corrosive chemical. This is unsafe. The Safety Data Sheet and risk assessment must identify compatible glove material, eye/face protection, clothing, emergency washing and other controls.

questions.prompt: Where does PPE normally sit in the Hierarchy of Controls?
questions.explanation: PPE is normally the final control level.

questions.prompt: What should happen before using PPE?
options: Inspect it and confirm suitability and fit
questions.explanation: PPE must be suitable, compatible, fitted and serviceable.

questions.prompt: Can every glove protect against every hazard?
options: No, selection must match the hazard
questions.explanation: PPE materials have specific capabilities and limitations.

lessons.title: Safe Systems of Work and Permit to Work
lessons.summary: This foundation module introduces the essential ideas every worker needs before starting or supporting workplace activities. It uses simple English, practical examples and short knowledge checks.

sections.heading: Safe System of Work
points: A safe system of work is a formal method for completing a task safely. It considers people, equipment, materials, environment, sequence, controls and emergencies. It may include a risk assessment, method statement, procedure, competent supervision and briefing.

sections.heading: Permit to Work
points: A permit to work is documented authorization for specified high-risk work under defined conditions and for a limited period. It does not make work safe by itself; all required controls must be implemented and verified.
Hot work
Confined-space entry
Electrical isolation
Excavation
Roof access or work at height where required
Line breaking or work on hazardous systems

sections.heading: Before, During and After Work
points: Confirm task, location, scope and validity.
Verify risk assessment and approved method.
Confirm competence, tools, equipment, PPE and supervision.
Complete required isolation, testing, barricading and emergency preparation.
Stop if conditions change or permit requirements cannot be met.
On completion, make the area safe and formally close or hand back the permit.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: A hot-work permit covers Area A, but the team moves to Area B. Stop work. The existing permit may not cover the new location or hazards and must be reviewed before restarting.

questions.prompt: What does a permit to work provide?
questions.explanation: A permit defines authorized work, conditions and limits.

questions.prompt: What should happen when conditions change?
questions.explanation: Changes may invalidate controls or authorization.

questions.prompt: Does a permit alone make work safe?
options: No, controls must be implemented and verified
questions.explanation: The permit cannot replace physical implementation of controls.

lessons.title: Safety Signs and Workplace Communication
lessons.summary: This foundation module introduces the essential ideas every worker needs before starting or supporting workplace activities. It uses simple English, practical examples and short knowledge checks.

sections.heading: Safety Sign Types
points: Prohibition: an action is not allowed, such as No Smoking.
Warning: a hazard or danger exists, such as High Voltage.
Mandatory: an action must be followed, such as Wear Eye Protection.
Safe condition: emergency exits, first aid or safe routes.
Fire equipment: extinguishers, hose reels or alarm points.

sections.heading: Other Communication Methods
points: Induction and task training.
Toolbox talks and pre-task briefings.
Risk assessments, method statements and permits.
Barricades, labels, tags and floor markings.
Radios and agreed hand signals.
Shift handovers, alerts and emergency alarms.

sections.heading: Effective Communication
points: Communication must be clear and suitable for language, literacy, noise and visibility conditions. Critical instructions should be confirmed through questions or repeat-back. Signs support controls but do not replace guarding, isolation, training or supervision.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: A crane operator cannot see the load and receives signals from two people. Stop the lift. One authorized signaler must be identified, communication agreed and emergency stop signals understood.

questions.prompt: What does a mandatory sign communicate?
options: An action that must be followed
questions.explanation: Mandatory signs identify required actions.

questions.prompt: Can a warning sign replace a machine guard?
options: No, it does not physically control the hazard
questions.explanation: A sign warns but does not isolate the hazard.

questions.prompt: How can understanding of a critical instruction be confirmed?
questions.explanation: Feedback confirms that the message was understood.

finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: Safety prevents injury, illness and other work-related harm.

finalAssessment.prompt: Which statement best defines a hazard?
options: Anything with potential to cause harm

finalAssessment.prompt: Risk is commonly evaluated using which two factors?
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: Likelihood and severity estimate probability and consequence.

finalAssessment.prompt: What should happen to a tool with a serious defect?
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: Defective tools must be controlled and reported.
Correct answer: Duties are shared but differ according to authority and role.

finalAssessment.prompt: What should a worker do if not trained for a task?
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: No one should perform work without required competence and authorization.

options: An event with potential for harm but no actual harm
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: A near miss caused no harm but had harmful potential.

options: The careless worker nearly killed us
At 10:15, a spanner fell from Level 2 into the barricaded area; work stopped
It was probably the supervisor's fault
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: Good reports use exact, neutral and verifiable facts.

finalAssessment.prompt: What should happen first when serious immediate danger is discovered?
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: Immediate danger requires prompt control, warning and reporting.

finalAssessment.prompt: What is normally the last level in the Hierarchy of Controls?
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: PPE is normally the final and least reliable level.

finalAssessment.prompt: During evacuation, where should workers go?
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: Assembly points support accountability and emergency control.

finalAssessment.prompt: Who should carry out electrical repairs?
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: Electrical repairs require qualified authorization.

finalAssessment.prompt: When may a casualty be moved?
options: Only when trained/necessary or leaving them creates greater danger
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: Unnecessary movement may worsen injuries; immediate danger may justify movement.

finalAssessment.prompt: When may workers re-enter after an emergency?
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: Only emergency control personnel may authorize re-entry.

finalAssessment.prompt: Why is PPE less reliable than elimination?
options: It depends on correct selection and use
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: PPE depends on correct selection, fit, use and maintenance.

finalAssessment.prompt: What must PPE selection be based on?
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: PPE must match the assessed hazard and task.

finalAssessment.prompt: What is a permit to work?
options: Authorization for specified work and conditions
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: A permit documents authorization, scope, controls and limits.

finalAssessment.prompt: What should happen if permit conditions change?
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: Changes may invalidate the permit and controls.

finalAssessment.prompt: Which sign states an action must be followed?
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: Mandatory signs state required actions.

finalAssessment.prompt: Who should signal a crane operator during a controlled lift?
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: One authorized signaler prevents conflicting instructions.

lessons.title: Introduction to Hazard Identification
lessons.summary: This module teaches a practical, systematic approach to identifying workplace hazards, evaluating risk, selecting controls, recording findings and reviewing effectiveness. It uses a generic 5x5 model for learning; organizations must apply their approved matrix, procedures and applicable legal requirements.

sections.heading: Learning Objectives
points: Explain proactive hazard identification.
Recognize why hazards must be found before harm occurs.
Identify information sources used during hazard identification.

sections.heading: What Hazard Identification Means
points: Hazard identification is the systematic process of finding conditions, activities, substances, equipment and behaviours that could cause injury, illness, damage or loss. It must cover routine, non-routine and emergency work.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
points: Finding and correcting hazards before an incident is more effective than reacting after harm. A strong process includes worker participation because workers often understand day-to-day conditions, task changes and practical control problems.

sections.heading: Useful Information Sources
points: Workplace inspections; task observation; worker consultation; incident, near-miss and illness records; equipment manuals; Safety Data Sheets; legal and client requirements; maintenance records; exposure monitoring; change-management reviews; and emergency planning.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: A workshop has no recent injuries, so management assumes it is safe. During inspection, workers identify a removed machine guard, damaged cable and blocked exit. Absence of injury does not prove absence of hazards; each finding requires immediate control and follow-up.

questions.prompt: What is hazard identification?
options: Systematically finding sources of potential harm
questions.explanation: It proactively finds conditions or activities that may cause harm.

questions.prompt: Which work must be considered?
questions.explanation: Hazards may arise in every operating condition.

questions.prompt: Why involve workers?
options: They remove the need for inspections
questions.explanation: Worker knowledge improves hazard recognition and practical controls.

lessons.title: Hazard, Unsafe Act and Unsafe Condition
lessons.summary: This module teaches a practical, systematic approach to identifying workplace hazards, evaluating risk, selecting controls, recording findings and reviewing effectiveness. It uses a generic 5x5 model for learning; organizations must apply their approved matrix, procedures and applicable legal requirements.

sections.heading: Learning Objectives
points: Distinguish the three terms.
Describe observations without blame.
Recognize underlying system factors.

sections.heading: Hazard
points: A hazard is anything with potential to cause harm, such as electricity, a moving vehicle, a chemical or an open edge.

sections.heading: Unsafe Condition
points: An unsafe condition is a physical or environmental state that increases risk, such as a missing guardrail, oil spill, defective tool or blocked exit.

sections.heading: Unsafe Act or Behaviour
points: An unsafe act is behaviour that departs from an established safe method, such as bypassing a guard or entering an exclusion zone. Investigations should not stop at blaming an individual; training, supervision, design, workload, tools and organizational pressures must also be examined.

sections.heading: Neutral Observation Language
points: Record what was seen: 'Worker entered the lifting exclusion zone while the load was suspended.' Avoid labels such as careless or stupid. Facts support fair investigation.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: A worker removes eye protection because goggles repeatedly fog. The act is unsafe, but the assessment must also examine ventilation, goggle selection, anti-fog options, task design, supervision and worker consultation.

questions.prompt: Which is an unsafe condition?
questions.explanation: A blocked exit is a dangerous physical condition.

questions.prompt: Which is an unsafe act?
options: Entering a barricaded area without authority
questions.explanation: The behaviour departs from the safe restriction.

questions.prompt: Why avoid blame-only investigation?
options: System factors may contribute and must be corrected
questions.explanation: Lasting prevention requires examination of underlying causes.

lessons.title: Methods of Identifying Hazards
lessons.summary: This module teaches a practical, systematic approach to identifying workplace hazards, evaluating risk, selecting controls, recording findings and reviewing effectiveness. It uses a generic 5x5 model for learning; organizations must apply their approved matrix, procedures and applicable legal requirements.

sections.heading: Learning Objectives
points: Use several identification methods.
Recognize less obvious health hazards.
Consider non-routine and changing work.

sections.heading: Workplace Inspection
points: Walk through the area using observation and a suitable checklist. Speak with workers and check access, equipment, substances, housekeeping, guarding, emergency arrangements and work practices.

sections.heading: Task Observation and JHA/JSA
points: Break the task into logical steps, identify hazards at each step, then select controls. Observe the real job rather than relying only on paperwork.

sections.heading: Review of Records
points: Use incidents, near misses, first-aid cases, occupational illness, maintenance defects, complaints and exposure data to find patterns.

sections.heading: Documents and Specialist Input
points: Review manuals, SDS, drawings, permits, monitoring results and applicable requirements. Obtain competent specialist advice when hazards such as structural stability, electricity, chemicals or occupational hygiene exceed local competence.

sections.heading: Change and Non-routine Review
points: Assess maintenance, start-up, shutdown, cleaning, breakdowns, temporary work, new equipment, new substances, weather and simultaneous operations.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: A team assesses normal machine operation but ignores cleaning. During cleaning, guards are open and stored energy remains. A separate non-routine review and safe isolation method are required.

questions.prompt: Which method examines each task step?
questions.explanation: A job hazard analysis connects hazards and controls to task steps.

questions.prompt: Which record can reveal recurring hazards?
questions.explanation: Near-miss trends can expose failed or missing controls.

questions.prompt: When is specialist advice needed?
options: Whenever no one wants to work
questions.explanation: Risk assessment must be supported by suitable competence.

lessons.title: Who Might Be Harmed and How
lessons.summary: This module teaches a practical, systematic approach to identifying workplace hazards, evaluating risk, selecting controls, recording findings and reviewing effectiveness. It uses a generic 5x5 model for learning; organizations must apply their approved matrix, procedures and applicable legal requirements.

sections.heading: Learning Objectives
points: Identify exposed groups.
Describe credible harm and exposure routes.
Consider vulnerable persons.

sections.heading: People to Consider
points: Employees, contractors, subcontractors, visitors, members of the public, drivers, cleaners, maintenance staff, emergency responders, remote workers and anyone affected by adjacent work.

sections.heading: Vulnerable or Higher-risk Groups
points: New or young workers, inexperienced persons, pregnant workers, people with disabilities or medical restrictions, lone workers, night workers, language/literacy limitations and persons unfamiliar with the site may need additional controls.

sections.heading: How Harm May Occur
points: State the exposure and consequence clearly: inhalation of silica dust may cause lung disease; contact with a live conductor may cause shock or burns; a falling object may strike persons below.

sections.heading: Exposure Pattern
points: Consider who is exposed, how often, for how long, by which route and how many people could be affected.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: Roof work is assessed only for installers. The revised assessment also considers people below, building occupants, delivery drivers, maintenance staff and rescuers, with exclusion zones, access control and communication.

questions.prompt: Who should a risk assessment consider?
questions.explanation: All potentially affected persons must be considered.

questions.prompt: Which group may need additional controls?
questions.explanation: Inexperience can increase vulnerability.

questions.prompt: Which description is clearest?
options: Inhalation of vapour may cause respiratory harm
questions.explanation: It identifies exposure route and possible harm.

lessons.title: Likelihood and Severity
lessons.summary: This module teaches a practical, systematic approach to identifying workplace hazards, evaluating risk, selecting controls, recording findings and reviewing effectiveness. It uses a generic 5x5 model for learning; organizations must apply their approved matrix, procedures and applicable legal requirements.

sections.heading: Learning Objectives
points: Rate likelihood and severity consistently.
Use evidence rather than guesswork.
Recognize limits of risk scores.

sections.heading: Likelihood
points: Likelihood estimates how probable harm is, considering exposure frequency and duration, number of people, task conditions, control reliability, human interaction and incident history.

sections.heading: Severity
points: Severity estimates the credible consequence, such as minor injury, lost-time injury, permanent disability, single fatality or multiple fatalities. Use a defined company matrix; labels vary between organizations.

sections.heading: Risk Rating
points: A common method multiplies Likelihood by Severity. The score helps prioritize action but does not replace professional judgment or legal requirements. A low probability of fatal harm still requires strong control.

sections.heading: Evidence and Consistency
points: Use observations, records, monitoring, manufacturer data and competent input. Document assumptions and apply the chosen matrix consistently.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: An open roof edge could cause a fatal fall. Even if workers approach it infrequently, severity remains very high. The edge requires effective protection rather than accepting a low-frequency exposure.

questions.prompt: What does likelihood estimate?
questions.explanation: Likelihood concerns how probable the event or exposure is.

questions.prompt: What does severity estimate?
questions.explanation: Severity addresses how serious the harm could be.

questions.prompt: Can a risk score replace judgment?
questions.explanation: Scores support decisions but cannot replace competent assessment.

lessons.title: Using a 5x5 Risk Matrix
lessons.summary: This module teaches a practical, systematic approach to identifying workplace hazards, evaluating risk, selecting controls, recording findings and reviewing effectiveness. It uses a generic 5x5 model for learning; organizations must apply their approved matrix, procedures and applicable legal requirements.

sections.heading: Learning Objectives
points: Calculate a basic 5x5 score.
Interpret bands using an approved matrix.
Avoid false precision.

sections.heading: Typical Scale
points: Likelihood and Severity may each be rated from 1 to 5. Example likelihood: Rare, Unlikely, Possible, Likely, Almost Certain. Example severity: Insignificant, Minor, Moderate, Major, Catastrophic. Always use the definitions approved by the organization.

sections.heading: Calculation
points: Risk score = Likelihood x Severity. Example: Likelihood 4 and Severity 5 produce 20. The organization's matrix determines whether that score is classified as High or Extreme and what action is required.

sections.heading: Action Principle
points: Higher risks normally require more urgent action and stronger authorization. Uncontrolled intolerable work must not start or continue.

sections.heading: Limitations
points: Numbers may create false confidence. Two assessors can choose different ratings unless definitions, evidence and competent review are used. Never lower a score merely to obtain approval.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: A lifting task is rated 2 x 5 = 10 after assuming barricades exist. Site inspection finds no barricade. The assessor must rate actual conditions, introduce interim control and reassess before work.

questions.prompt: What is 4 x 5?
questions.explanation: The basic product is 20.

questions.prompt: Which matrix definitions should be used?
questions.explanation: Consistent approved definitions are essential.

questions.prompt: What if an intolerable risk is uncontrolled?
questions.explanation: Work requires effective control before proceeding.

lessons.title: Initial and Residual Risk
lessons.summary: This module teaches a practical, systematic approach to identifying workplace hazards, evaluating risk, selecting controls, recording findings and reviewing effectiveness. It uses a generic 5x5 model for learning; organizations must apply their approved matrix, procedures and applicable legal requirements.

sections.heading: Learning Objectives
points: Distinguish initial and residual risk.
Assess controls honestly.
Recognize that risk cannot be transferred to paperwork.

sections.heading: Initial Risk
points: Initial risk is the level assessed before proposed additional controls. Company systems differ on whether existing controls are included; the selected definition must be stated and used consistently.

sections.heading: Residual Risk
points: Residual risk is the remaining risk after specified controls are implemented. It must reflect controls that are suitable, available, verified and maintained - not controls that exist only on paper.

sections.heading: Control Effect on Ratings
points: Many controls reduce likelihood. Some controls can reduce severity, for example separating people from an energy source or limiting hazardous inventory. Do not automatically reduce both values.

sections.heading: Verification
points: Before accepting residual risk, confirm control ownership, completion date, competence, inspection, monitoring and communication. If controls fail or conditions change, reassess.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: A roof-edge task is initially 4 x 5 = 20. A designed guardrail may reduce likelihood significantly while fall severity remains 5. The residual rating must use the approved matrix and verified guardrail condition.

questions.prompt: What is residual risk?
questions.explanation: It is the remaining assessed risk after controls.

questions.prompt: Should both likelihood and severity always be reduced?
questions.explanation: A control may affect one factor but not the other.

questions.prompt: Can an unimplemented future control justify a low residual rating?
questions.explanation: Residual ratings must reflect real, verified controls.

lessons.title: Selecting Controls Using the Hierarchy
lessons.summary: This module teaches a practical, systematic approach to identifying workplace hazards, evaluating risk, selecting controls, recording findings and reviewing effectiveness. It uses a generic 5x5 model for learning; organizations must apply their approved matrix, procedures and applicable legal requirements.

sections.heading: Learning Objectives
points: Apply the control hierarchy.
Select controls for the actual task.
Assign and verify actions.

sections.heading: Preferred Order
points: Consider elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls and PPE in that order. Elimination, substitution and engineering are generally more reliable because they depend less on continuous human action.

sections.heading: Control Quality
points: Controls should be specific, practical, compatible with the work, maintained and capable of reducing exposure. 'Be careful' is not an adequate control.

sections.heading: Interim and Permanent Controls
points: Use interim protection when permanent solutions take time, but track permanent action. Urgent serious hazards require immediate protection or work stoppage.

sections.heading: Action Planning
points: Record the action, responsible person, target date, resources, verification method and completion status. Consult workers before finalizing practical controls.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: Pedestrians share a route with forklifts. A PPE-only response is weak. Better controls include eliminating shared movement, physical separation, one-way routes, barriers, controlled crossings, speed control, trained operators and high-visibility clothing as supporting PPE.

questions.prompt: Which control is preferred over training alone?
questions.explanation: Engineering separation is less dependent on behaviour.

questions.prompt: Is 'be careful' a sufficient control?
questions.explanation: Controls must be specific and effective.

questions.prompt: What must an action plan include?
questions.explanation: Ownership and timing support completion and verification.

lessons.title: Recording and Reviewing Risk Assessments
lessons.summary: This module teaches a practical, systematic approach to identifying workplace hazards, evaluating risk, selecting controls, recording findings and reviewing effectiveness. It uses a generic 5x5 model for learning; organizations must apply their approved matrix, procedures and applicable legal requirements.

sections.heading: Learning Objectives
points: Record significant findings clearly.
Communicate controls.
Identify review triggers.

sections.heading: What to Record
points: Task and location; persons at risk; hazards and possible harm; existing controls; initial rating; further controls; action owner and target date; residual rating; assessor, approval, date and review information according to the organization system.

sections.heading: Communication and Implementation
points: A signed form is not enough. Relevant people must understand controls before work. Verify implementation through inspection, supervision, observation and monitoring.

sections.heading: Review Triggers
points: Review after incidents or near misses; changes in people, process, equipment, substances, layout or law; evidence controls are ineffective; new information; significant weather or site changes; and at the defined periodic interval.

sections.heading: Document Control
points: Use current approved versions, clear revision status and accessible records. Withdraw obsolete versions and preserve required records.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: A risk assessment is signed but workers have not seen it and the equipment has changed. Stop and review the assessment, involve the team, update controls and brief everyone before restarting.

questions.prompt: Is a signature alone evidence controls work?
questions.explanation: Implementation and verification are required.

questions.prompt: Which event triggers review?
questions.explanation: Changes can introduce new hazards or invalidate controls.

questions.prompt: What should happen to obsolete versions?
questions.explanation: Document control prevents outdated instructions.

lessons.title: Practical Risk Assessment Scenario
lessons.summary: This module teaches a practical, systematic approach to identifying workplace hazards, evaluating risk, selecting controls, recording findings and reviewing effectiveness. It uses a generic 5x5 model for learning; organizations must apply their approved matrix, procedures and applicable legal requirements.

sections.heading: Learning Objectives
points: Apply the complete process.
Write task-specific controls.
Evaluate residual risk after verification.

sections.heading: Scenario: Guardrail Installation on a Roof
points: The team will deliver materials, access the roof, move components, install guardrails using hand and power tools, and clear the area. Persons at risk include installers, occupants, people below, visitors and rescuers.

sections.heading: Key Hazards
points: Falls from edges or fragile surfaces; dropped objects; unsafe access; manual handling; power tools; electricity; weather; poor communication; restricted rescue; and unauthorized entry below.

sections.heading: Control Strategy
points: Where practicable, eliminate exposure by pre-assembly at ground level. Verify roof condition, drawings and safe access. Provide collective edge protection or an approved fall-protection system, exclusion zone, secured tools/materials, mechanical handling aids, inspected tools, competent workers, permit/briefing, weather limits and a task-specific rescue plan.

sections.heading: Assessment and Review
points: Use the approved matrix to rate actual initial conditions. Assign actions and verify them before work. Rate residual risk without automatically reducing severity. Monitor the task and stop if access, weather, roof condition, equipment, personnel or scope changes.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: During installation, wind increases and loose packaging begins to move. The supervisor stops work, secures materials, checks the defined weather limits and reviews conditions before authorizing restart.

questions.prompt: Who may be harmed by dropped tools?
options: People below and others entering the area
questions.explanation: The assessment must include everyone exposed below.

questions.prompt: What should happen when wind exceeds the safe limit?
questions.explanation: Changed weather can invalidate controls.

questions.prompt: What must happen before residual risk is accepted?
questions.explanation: Residual risk must reflect implemented controls.

finalAssessment.prompt: What is the purpose of hazard identification?
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: Find potential harm before incidents
Correct answer: Routine, non-routine and emergencies
Correct answer: To support fair evidence-based review

finalAssessment.prompt: Which method breaks work into steps?
Which source can reveal recurring hazards?
Who should be considered in an assessment?
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: Anyone who may be affected

finalAssessment.prompt: Which group may need additional controls?

finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: The approved organizational matrix

options: Risk before proposed additional controls under the stated system
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: Risk before proposed additional controls under the stated system
Correct answer: Risk remaining after implemented controls

finalAssessment.prompt: Should likelihood and severity always both reduce?
What is the highest control level?
What should an action record include?
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: Owner and target date

options: No - controls must be communicated and implemented
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: No - controls must be communicated and implemented

finalAssessment.prompt: What should happen to obsolete documents?
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: Be withdrawn from active use

finalAssessment.prompt: Who is at risk from dropped tools?
What should happen when conditions change significantly?
When may residual risk be accepted?
options: After controls are implemented and verified
When the form is signed only
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: After controls are implemented and verified

title: Core Workplace Safety Practices
description: This module introduces ten essential workplace safety practices. It is generic learning content and must be applied together with site-specific risk assessments, approved procedures, competent supervision, manufacturer instructions and applicable legal requirements.

lessons.title: Personal Protective Equipment
lessons.summary: This module introduces ten essential workplace safety practices. It is generic learning content and must be applied together with site-specific risk assessments, approved procedures, competent supervision, manufacturer instructions and applicable legal requirements.

sections.heading: Core Learning
points: PPE reduces exposure but does not remove the hazard. Select it from the risk assessment after considering higher controls.
Common PPE includes head, eye, face, hand, foot, hearing, respiratory, high-visibility and fall-protection equipment. Each item protects against specific hazards.
Confirm suitability, certification where required, correct fit, compatibility, pre-use condition, cleaning, storage, inspection and replacement. Never modify PPE.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: A worker uses general gloves with a corrosive liquid. Stop and check the SDS and assessment for compatible glove material, eye/face protection, clothing and emergency washing.

questions.prompt: What determines PPE selection?
questions.explanation: PPE must match the actual hazard and exposure.

questions.prompt: Can PPE replace elimination?
questions.explanation: Higher controls should be used where practicable.

questions.prompt: What should happen before use?
questions.explanation: PPE must be suitable and serviceable.

lessons.title: Housekeeping, Slips and Trips
lessons.summary: This module introduces ten essential workplace safety practices. It is generic learning content and must be applied together with site-specific risk assessments, approved procedures, competent supervision, manufacturer instructions and applicable legal requirements.

sections.heading: Core Learning
points: Slips may result from wet, oily, dusty or unsuitable surfaces. Trips may result from cables, waste, uneven floors, poor lighting or blocked routes.
Use suitable flooring and drainage, prevent leaks, clean spills promptly, route cables safely, provide lighting, segregate storage and keep access, stairs and exits clear.
Housekeeping is continuous. Assign responsibility, provide waste facilities and inspect work areas during and after tasks. Barricade a spill until fully controlled.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: Oil leaks into a walkway. Stop access, control the source, barricade, clean with the correct spill materials, dispose of waste properly and verify the surface is safe.

questions.prompt: What should happen to a spill?
options: Control, barricade and clean it promptly
questions.explanation: Immediate control prevents exposure.

questions.prompt: Where may materials be stored?
questions.explanation: Storage must not obstruct safe access.

questions.prompt: When is housekeeping required?
questions.explanation: Conditions change throughout work.

lessons.title: Manual Handling and Ergonomics
lessons.summary: This module introduces ten essential workplace safety practices. It is generic learning content and must be applied together with site-specific risk assessments, approved procedures, competent supervision, manufacturer instructions and applicable legal requirements.

sections.heading: Core Learning
points: Manual handling includes lifting, lowering, pushing, pulling, carrying or moving a load by hand or bodily force. Repetition, force, posture, load and environment affect risk.
Avoid hazardous handling where practicable. Use hoists, trolleys, pallet trucks, lift tables or redesign. Reduce weight, distance, frequency and awkward reaches.
If manual handling remains, plan the route, obtain a secure grip, keep the load close, avoid twisting, coordinate team lifts and stop if the load is unstable or beyond capability.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: Two workers try to carry a long heavy component up stairs. Reassess and use suitable mechanical assistance or a planned lifting method rather than relying on strength.

questions.prompt: What is the preferred first step?
questions.explanation: Eliminating the lift is more reliable.

questions.prompt: Which increases risk?
questions.explanation: Twisting increases musculoskeletal load.

questions.prompt: What if a load is beyond capability?
options: Stop and obtain assistance or equipment
questions.explanation: The task must be redesigned or assisted.

lessons.title: Hand and Power Tool Safety
lessons.summary: This module introduces ten essential workplace safety practices. It is generic learning content and must be applied together with site-specific risk assessments, approved procedures, competent supervision, manufacturer instructions and applicable legal requirements.

sections.heading: Core Learning
points: Use the correct tool for the task. Inspect handles, guards, switches, discs, bits, cables, plugs, hoses and accessories before use.
Do not remove guards or bypass dead-man controls. Secure the work, maintain stable posture, control sparks and flying particles, and keep others outside the hazard area.
Remove defective tools from service, identify them clearly and allow only authorized competent persons to repair. Isolate energy before changing accessories according to instructions.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: A grinder has a missing guard and cracked disc. Stop, isolate and tag it out. Replace/repair through the authorized process and inspect before return to service.

questions.prompt: May a grinder run without its guard?
questions.explanation: The guard is a required engineering control.

questions.prompt: Who repairs defective tools?
questions.explanation: Unauthorized repairs create additional hazards.

questions.prompt: What happens to a cracked disc?
questions.explanation: Damaged abrasive wheels may fail violently.

lessons.title: Electrical Safety
lessons.summary: This module introduces ten essential workplace safety practices. It is generic learning content and must be applied together with site-specific risk assessments, approved procedures, competent supervision, manufacturer instructions and applicable legal requirements.

sections.heading: Core Learning
points: Electrical hazards include contact with live parts, damaged insulation, poor grounding, overloaded circuits, wet conditions, overhead lines and unauthorized work.
De-energize and isolate where practicable. Verify isolation using the approved procedure and suitable test equipment. Electrical work requires authorized qualified persons.
Inspect portable equipment, use appropriate protection devices, keep connections dry, manage cables and maintain safe clearance from overhead or buried services.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: A cable joint lies in standing water. Stop use, isolate safely, control access and arrange inspection by an authorized electrical person.

questions.prompt: Who performs electrical repairs?
questions.explanation: Electrical work requires competence and authorization.

questions.prompt: What should happen near standing water?
options: Stop and control the electrical hazard
questions.explanation: Water can increase shock risk.

questions.prompt: Can isolation be assumed?
questions.explanation: Verification prevents contact with live energy.

lessons.title: Fire Safety and Hot Work
lessons.summary: This module introduces ten essential workplace safety practices. It is generic learning content and must be applied together with site-specific risk assessments, approved procedures, competent supervision, manufacturer instructions and applicable legal requirements.

sections.heading: Core Learning
points: Fire needs fuel, oxygen and an ignition source. Control combustible material, flammable storage, electrical faults, smoking and hot-work sparks.

Hot work requires the applicable authorization, area inspection, removal or protection of combustibles, suitable extinguishing equipment, ventilation, fire watch where required and post-work monitoring.
Raise the alarm and evacuate. Use an extinguisher only if trained, authorized, the fire is small, the correct unit is available and a safe escape remains.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: Grinding sparks travel beyond the barricade toward packaging. Stop work, extend control of the spark path, remove/protect combustibles and revalidate hot-work controls.

questions.prompt: What three elements support fire?
questions.explanation: Removing an element can prevent or control fire.

questions.prompt: What if sparks reach combustibles?
questions.explanation: Uncontrolled ignition exposure requires stoppage.

questions.prompt: When may an extinguisher be used?
questions.explanation: Personal safety and evacuation come first.

lessons.title: Work at Height
lessons.summary: This module introduces ten essential workplace safety practices. It is generic learning content and must be applied together with site-specific risk assessments, approved procedures, competent supervision, manufacturer instructions and applicable legal requirements.

sections.heading: Core Learning
points: Plan work at height using the hierarchy: avoid height where practicable, prevent falls with collective protection, then minimize distance and consequences using suitable systems.
Verify safe access, platforms, edges, openings, fragile surfaces, weather, falling objects, competence, inspection, anchorage and rescue before work.
Personal fall arrest requires compatible equipment, adequate clearance and a prompt rescue plan. A harness alone does not make the work safe.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: Installers reach an unprotected roof edge with no rescue plan. Stop work and provide approved access, edge protection or designed fall protection, exclusion below and rescue readiness.

questions.prompt: What is preferred first?
questions.explanation: Avoidance eliminates fall exposure.

questions.prompt: Does a harness alone make work safe?
questions.explanation: A complete compatible system and rescue are needed.

questions.prompt: What must be checked below?
questions.explanation: People below may be struck.

lessons.title: Lifting Operations
lessons.summary: This module introduces ten essential workplace safety practices. It is generic learning content and must be applied together with site-specific risk assessments, approved procedures, competent supervision, manufacturer instructions and applicable legal requirements.

sections.heading: Core Learning
points: Plan lifting by competent persons. Confirm load weight, centre of gravity, lifting points, equipment capacity, configuration, ground conditions, route and environmental limits.
Use certified/inspected cranes and accessories, competent operators, riggers and signalers, suitable rigging, tag lines where appropriate and a controlled exclusion zone.
Never stand under suspended loads or enter the lifting zone without authorization. Stop for loss of communication, instability, people/equipment intrusion or changed conditions.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: A forklift enters the crane exclusion zone while a load is suspended. The signaler gives the stop signal; lifting resumes only after the area is clear and controlled.

questions.prompt: Who plans the lift?
questions.explanation: Planning requires suitable lifting competence.

questions.prompt: May anyone stand under a suspended load?
questions.explanation: Suspended loads can fall without warning.

questions.prompt: What if communication is lost?
questions.explanation: Reliable communication is essential.

lessons.title: Mobile Plant and Pedestrian Safety
lessons.summary: This module introduces ten essential workplace safety practices. It is generic learning content and must be applied together with site-specific risk assessments, approved procedures, competent supervision, manufacturer instructions and applicable legal requirements.

sections.heading: Core Learning
points: Separate vehicles and pedestrians using site layout, barriers, one-way routes, controlled crossings and designated walkways wherever practicable.
Use trained authorized operators, pre-use checks, suitable visibility aids, speed limits, parking controls and a trained banksman where the assessment requires one.
Pedestrians must use defined routes and never enter blind spots or operating zones without communication and authorization. Mobile phones and distraction increase risk.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: A reversing delivery vehicle has limited visibility and people cross behind it. Stop movement, clear the area and use the planned route and competent banksman.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest traffic control?
questions.explanation: Separation reduces interaction.

questions.prompt: Who operates mobile plant?
questions.explanation: Operator competence and authorization are required.

questions.prompt: What should happen in a blind spot?
questions.explanation: Operators may not see pedestrians.

lessons.title: Chemical Safety and SDS
lessons.summary: This module introduces ten essential workplace safety practices. It is generic learning content and must be applied together with site-specific risk assessments, approved procedures, competent supervision, manufacturer instructions and applicable legal requirements.

sections.heading: Core Learning
points: Chemical exposure may occur by inhalation, skin/eye contact, ingestion or injection. Process-generated dust, fume, vapour, mist and gas must also be assessed.

Use current labels and Safety Data Sheets. The standardized SDS provides identification, hazards, composition, first aid, firefighting, spill response, handling/storage, exposure controls and other information.
Eliminate or substitute where possible, use closed systems and ventilation, control quantities and storage, segregate incompatibles, plan spills and select PPE from the assessment and SDS.

sections.heading: Practical Scenario
points: An unlabelled liquid is found in a drink bottle. Do not use or smell it. Isolate the container and have it identified and managed under the chemical procedure.

questions.prompt: What should happen to an unknown chemical?
questions.explanation: Unknown substances require controlled identification.

questions.prompt: Where is hazard and first-aid information found?
questions.explanation: The SDS communicates chemical safety information.

questions.prompt: Is PPE the only chemical control?
questions.explanation: Substitution and engineering controls are preferred where practicable.

finalAssessment.prompt: What is the correct spill response?
options: Control source, barricade and clean safely
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: Control source, barricade and clean safely

finalAssessment.prompt: What is preferred for hazardous manual handling?
May a guard be removed from a power tool?
What happens to a defective tool?
What if hot-work sparks reach combustibles?
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: Stop and correct controls

finalAssessment.prompt: What is the first work-at-height option?
What does fall arrest also require?
May people stand under suspended loads?
What if lift communication is lost?
What should pedestrians do near blind spots?
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: Keep out and communicate

finalAssessment.prompt: What should happen to an unknown liquid?
finalAssessment.explanation: Correct answer: Isolate and identify safely
